#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when it pulls in more than you declared*
This scenario demonstrates the fundamental mechanism of transitive dependency resolution in sbt: you declare one library and get its whole subtree.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **sbt 1.12**, which uses the **Coursier** resolver (the default since sbt 1.3). On sbt 1.x the older Ivy engine can still be selected with `useCoursier := false`; under Ivy, resolution edge cases differ and Ivy-only settings such as `conflictManager` apply (Coursier ignores them). `dependencyTree` is built in since **sbt 1.4**; earlier versions need the sbt-dependency-graph plugin. sbt 2.0 (June 2026) keeps these resolution rules, removes the Ivy opt-out, adds native BOM import, and turns Test-configuration eviction warnings into errors; the demos here target sbt 1.x.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] --> LibA[lib-a:1.0.0]
    LibA --> LibB[lib-b:1.0.0]
    LibB --> LibC[lib-c:1.0.0]
```

```{.scala include="build.sbt" snippet="s1-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
Declaring `lib-a` automatically puts its transitive dependencies `lib-b` and `lib-c` on the classpath.

#### ! Why
Coursier reads the POM of every artifact it fetches and recursively resolves the dependencies declared there. You declare the roots of the graph; the resolver walks the rest. This is what makes a one-line declaration pull in a chain of libraries you never named.

#### ! Fix
There is nothing to fix; this is the intended behaviour. Developers sometimes add transitive dependencies to `libraryDependencies` "to be sure" they are present. That is unnecessary unless your code imports classes from those libraries directly, in which case declaring them is correct: a dependency you compile against should be one you declare.

#### ! Risk
* LOW Declaring only the libraries you import and trusting resolution for the rest.
* MEDIUM Declaring transitives "to be safe"; the extra declarations later shadow what the real owner of the dependency wanted (see SB2).
* HIGH Assuming a small declaration means a small classpath. One library can bring hundreds of JARs, each a potential conflict and a potential CVE.

#### ! Control
Trust transitive resolution and keep `libraryDependencies` to the libraries your code actually uses. Review the full tree with `sbt dependencyTree` whenever you add a dependency.

#### ! Check

**Fast check:** `sbt dependencyTree`

**What to look for:** A clean chain `lib-a` → `lib-b` → `lib-c` with no `(evicted by: …)` markers.

**Conclusion:** The graph resolves exactly as the POMs describe it.

#### ! Scales
Transitive resolution is the only way modern software development scales; without it you would manage hundreds of JARs by hand. The cost is that adding one small library can pull in a large tree of other libraries, and every node in that tree is a candidate for a version conflict (SB2) or a security finding.

#### ! Takeaway
sbt resolves dependencies transitively. You declare the roots; Coursier finds the rest of the tree.

#### ! Wild

Declaring `spark-core` in a Scala project brings in well over a hundred transitive artifacts: Hadoop, Netty, Jackson, Guava, Avro, Parquet and their own subtrees. Nobody declares those, yet every one of them ends up on the classpath, and most Spark "dependency hell" stories (SB2, SB6) begin with a second library that brings a different version of one of them. Run `sbt dependencyTree` once on a fresh Spark project to see how much of your application you did not write.
